items.title: The Sahara was a green savannah 6,000 years ago
items.claim: Around 6,000 years ago, what is now the world's largest hot desert was something quite different. What was it?

options.text: It was already a desert; the Sahara has been arid for over 100,000 years
It was a savannah and grassland with lakes, rivers and human settlement — the 'African Humid Period'
It was a tropical rainforest like the Amazon today
It was covered by a shallow sea connected to the Mediterranean

items.reveal:
The African Humid Period lasted roughly 14,500 to 5,000 years ago. Cave paintings at Tassili n'Ajjer in Algeria show people herding cattle, swimming, and hunting hippos.

The cause was an orbital wobble — a stronger summer monsoon driven by changes in Earth's tilt and precession (Milankovitch cycles). When the monsoon retreated, the region desertified rapidly. Lake Chad was once larger than the Caspian Sea ('Lake Megachad').
items.why: Climate zones feel permanent on a human timescale. They are not. The Sahara's transformation in a few millennia is a reminder that 'natural' is just a snapshot of an unstable system.

items.title: Britain's climate is anomalously warm for its latitude
items.claim: London sits at 51 degrees North — the same latitude as Calgary, Canada (winters of -30 C). Why is London so much warmer?

options.text: The Gulf Stream and the wider North Atlantic Current transport tropical heat northward, with prevailing westerlies carrying it onshore
The North Sea acts as a giant heat reservoir from summer
Britain receives more solar radiation due to cloud cover patterns
The Jet Stream alone is responsible

items.reveal:
The Gulf Stream originates in the Gulf of Mexico, feeds the North Atlantic Current, and as it cools and becomes saltier, sinks near Iceland and Greenland — driving the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC). The energy transfer is roughly 1.3 petawatts, about 10,000 times UK electricity demand.

The AMOC has weakened measurably since the mid-20th century. A collapse would cool Britain dramatically while warming the tropics — a non-linear climate flip.
items.why: Climate is not just latitude. Ocean circulation is one of the largest energy-redistribution systems on the planet, and it's not guaranteed to keep running.

items.title: The Mediterranean Sea evaporated almost completely 5.96 million years ago
items.claim: The Mediterranean dried into a system of hypersaline lakes during the Messinian Salinity Crisis. How did it refill?

options.text: Slowly, over millions of years, from rainfall and river input
The Strait of Gibraltar breached and the Atlantic flooded back in possibly as little as months to a few years (the Zanclean flood)
Sea levels rose globally during a warm interglacial and topped the sill
Volcanic activity reopened the Sicilian connection to the Indian Ocean

items.reveal:
Tectonic uplift closed the Strait of Gibraltar around 6 million years ago. The Mediterranean evaporated, leaving a salt layer up to 2 km thick (still exploited today). When Gibraltar breached at the Zanclean (5.33 Ma), water poured in at an estimated 100 million cubic metres per second, with sea level rising by metres per day.

Garcia-Castellanos et al. (Nature, 2009) modelled the flood and concluded it could have refilled the basin in months to about two years.
items.why: The slow-geology stereotype is wrong. Geological events include some of the most violent, rapid changes the planet has ever seen. Catastrophism and uniformitarianism both have a place.

items.title: The Himalayas rise faster than they erode — but only just
items.claim: The Himalayas are uplifting at around 5-10 mm per year. What does this rate compare to?

options.text: Erosion is negligible; the mountains simply keep growing
Erosion roughly matches uplift in many parts of the range — the visible rate of height gain is only the difference
Erosion outpaces uplift, so the Himalayas are slowly shrinking
The mountains have been at their current height for 10 million years

items.reveal:
The India-Eurasia collision (started around 50 Ma) drives uplift. Monsoonal rainfall, glacier carving and river incision — especially by the Indus and the Brahmaputra — remove rock at comparable rates.

This is the 'aneurysm' or 'tectonic aneurysm' model: in places like Nanga Parbat, intense focused erosion actually accelerates uplift by removing load. Mountains are dynamic balance points, not static features.
items.why: Landscapes look permanent. They are conveyor belts running at millimetres per year, where the visible shape is the residual of two enormous, competing processes.

items.title: The Amazon used to flow the other way
items.claim: Today the Amazon flows from the Andes east into the Atlantic. What did it do before the Andes rose?

options.text: It always flowed east; the basin's shape has been stable for 100 million years
It drained westward into the Pacific until the Andes rose and reversed the gradient around 10 million years ago
It split into two systems, one east and one west, until tectonic activity merged them
It originally flowed north into the Caribbean

items.reveal:
Through the Cretaceous and early Cenozoic, the proto-Amazon drained westward into the Pacific. As the Andes uplifted from around 65 Ma but accelerated after 23 Ma, the western outlet was blocked. A vast inland wetland system (the Pebas system) developed in what is now western Amazonia.

By roughly 10-11 Ma, the river had cut through to the Atlantic and reversed. Hoorn et al. (Science, 2010) reconstructed the history from sediment cores.
items.why: Rivers feel like fixed features of geography. They are the temporary result of whatever tectonic surface is currently tilting. Change the tilt, change the flow.

items.title: Earth's magnetic north pole is racing toward Siberia
items.claim: Since the 1990s, the magnetic north pole has been moving from Arctic Canada toward Siberia. How fast?

options.text: About 1 km per year — barely perceptible
About 50-60 km per year during the 2000s, fast enough that the World Magnetic Model has needed unscheduled updates
About 500 km per year — already imminent reversal
It is stationary; only the geographic pole moves

items.reveal:
Through the 20th century the magnetic north pole drifted at roughly 10-15 km/year. From around 1990 it accelerated to 50-60 km/year. The British Geological Survey and NOAA released an unscheduled update to the World Magnetic Model in February 2019 because the error margins for navigation were being exceeded.

The last full geomagnetic reversal (Brunhes-Matuyama) was about 780,000 years ago. Reversals appear to take 1,000-10,000 years to complete and are not predictable from short-term drift.
items.why: The 'static Earth' model breaks down on geological scales — but also on human ones. Aviation charts, GPS backup systems and even some animal navigation depend on assumptions that are quietly being rewritten.

items.title: The Pacific Ring of Fire produces around 90% of the world's earthquakes
items.claim: What fraction of global seismic and volcanic activity occurs around the Pacific Rim?

options.text: About 20% — earthquakes are evenly distributed globally
Around 90% of the world's earthquakes and about 75% of active volcanoes occur around the Ring of Fire, a 40,000 km horseshoe of subduction zones
About 50% of earthquakes but only 10% of volcanoes
Almost all earthquakes globally — the rest occur only in Iceland

items.reveal:
The USGS records around 90% of earthquakes (and about 80% of the largest) along the Ring of Fire. It tracks the boundaries of the Pacific Plate against the Eurasian, North American, Philippine, Cocos, Nazca and Australian plates.

Major events on the Ring include the 1960 Valdivia earthquake (Chile, magnitude 9.5 — the largest ever recorded), the 1964 Alaska earthquake (9.2), the 2004 Sumatra-Andaman (9.1) and the 2011 Tohoku event (9.0). Mount St Helens (1980), Pinatubo (1991) and Krakatoa (1883) are all Ring volcanoes.
items.why: Hazard distribution is not random. It follows tectonic structure, and the implications for hazard planning — from Tokyo's building codes to Chile's tsunami warnings — depend on understanding why.

items.title: Tsunamis can cross the Pacific in under 24 hours
items.claim: How fast does a tsunami wave travel in the deep ocean?

options.text: Around 30 km/h, similar to wind waves
Around 700-900 km/h in deep water (jet airliner speed), slowing to tens of km/h as it shoals near coasts
The speed of sound in water (around 5,400 km/h)
Independent of water depth — always around 100 km/h

items.reveal:
Tsunami speed in open ocean is approximately √(g × h), where g is gravity (9.8 m/s²) and h is water depth. At 4,000 m, that gives around 700 km/h. The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami hit Sri Lanka and India about 2 hours after the Sumatra earthquake; Somalia, 5,000 km away, was hit about 7 hours later.

In deep ocean the wave height is usually under a metre and almost invisible. As depth decreases at coasts, energy compresses vertically and the wave can grow to tens of metres. The Pacific Tsunami Warning Center (Honolulu) uses DART buoys to detect waves.
items.why: The deep-ocean speed gives time for warnings across ocean basins but not for nearby coasts. Tsunami planning is therefore radically different at distance versus near the source — minutes versus hours.

items.title: Major volcanic eruptions inject ash into the stratosphere
items.claim: How high can a large eruption column reach?

options.text: Up to 5 km — high but contained in the troposphere
Plinian eruptions can exceed 30-40 km, well into the stratosphere — Mount Pinatubo (1991) reached around 35 km
Only the visible smoke is observable
No eruption has reached the stratosphere in recorded history

items.reveal:
Plinian eruptions (named after Pliny the Younger's description of Vesuvius in 79 CE) drive ash and sulphate aerosols into the stratosphere, where they can spread globally and remain for years. Pinatubo (June 1991) cooled global temperatures by around 0.5°C for 18 months.

Tambora (1815, VEI 7) caused the 'Year Without a Summer' (1816) — crop failures across Europe and North America, snow in June. Krakatoa (1883, VEI 6) produced spectacular sunsets globally. Toba (around 74,000 years ago, VEI 8) may have caused a population bottleneck in early humans.
items.why: Volcanic forcing is one of the strongest natural climate drivers on year-to-decade scales. Climate models calibrate against these events because the signal is large and well-dated.

items.title: Aftershocks can be larger than the original quake
items.claim: What is the technical relationship between a mainshock and aftershocks?

options.text: Aftershocks are always smaller than the mainshock

If a later event is larger than the original, it is retrospectively reclassified as the mainshock and the earlier event becomes a foreshock — so by definition the named mainshock is the largest in the sequence
Aftershocks are unrelated to mainshocks and randomly distributed
Aftershocks always occur within 24 hours

items.reveal:
Bath's law gives the largest aftershock as typically 1.2 magnitudes smaller than the mainshock. Omori's law (1894) gives the rate as decaying as 1/t. Aftershocks can continue for years after large events.

The 2011 Christchurch earthquake (magnitude 6.3, 22 February) was an aftershock of the September 2010 Darfield earthquake (7.1). Because the Christchurch event was smaller, it kept the aftershock label — but it killed 185 people because it was shallower and closer to the city.
items.why: Naming conventions can obscure danger. The aftershock label can sound like 'less hazardous' when the geometry of the event matters more than its magnitude.

items.title: Yellowstone has erupted as a supervolcano roughly every 600,000 years
items.claim: What is the recurrence interval of major Yellowstone caldera eruptions?

options.text: Every 10,000 years — overdue many times over
The last three major caldera-forming eruptions were around 2.1 million, 1.3 million and 631,000 years ago — an average interval of around 725,000 years, with no implied 'due date'
Every century — but eruptions have been small
Yellowstone has never been a supervolcano

items.reveal:
USGS Yellowstone Volcano Observatory data: Huckleberry Ridge (2.1 Ma), Mesa Falls (1.3 Ma), Lava Creek (631 ka). The last lava flow was 70,000 years ago. The current scientific consensus is that Yellowstone shows no signs of an imminent eruption.

Toba (Sumatra, around 74,000 years ago) ejected around 2,800 km³ of material — the largest eruption in the last 25 million years. The Yellowstone Lava Creek eruption ejected around 1,000 km³.

A VEI 8 eruption today would devastate North America with ashfall and disrupt global climate for years.
items.why: 'Overdue' supervolcano narratives misuse averages. Three datapoints do not establish a periodic schedule — and absent any geophysical signal of imminent eruption, the right answer is 'we don't know when, but not soon'.

items.title: Pompeii's victims were killed by heat, not ash
items.claim: What killed most Pompeii victims in 79 CE?

options.text: Suffocation by ash inhalation over hours
Pyroclastic flows (and surges) of around 300°C+ killed victims almost instantly — many bodies show signs of thermal shock and characteristic 'pugilistic' postures
Lava flows engulfed the town
Most survived; only a handful were killed

items.reveal:
Pliny the Younger described Vesuvius's eruption in letters to Tacitus (his uncle Pliny the Elder died at Stabiae). Modern analysis (Mastrolorenzo et al., 2010) showed pyroclastic surge temperatures of 250-300°C — instant death for those in their path.

The famous body casts were made by Giuseppe Fiorelli from 1863 by pouring plaster into voids left by decomposed bodies in the hardened ash. The town was buried under 4-6 metres of ash and pumice. Around 2,000 bodies have been found at Pompeii; perhaps 13,000 lived in the town.
items.why: The popular image of slow ash suffocation is wrong. Pyroclastic flows are the deadliest volcanic hazard precisely because they leave no time to react — a lesson built into modern volcanic risk planning.

items.title: River discharge is measured in cubic metres per second
items.claim: What does river discharge actually measure?

options.text: The depth of water in metres
Volume of water passing a point per unit time, typically m³/s (cumecs) — the product of cross-sectional area and mean velocity
The speed of water at the surface
The total water in the river basin

items.reveal:
Discharge Q = A × v, where A is cross-sectional area (m²) and v is mean velocity (m/s). The Thames at Kingston averages around 65 m³/s. The Amazon at its mouth averages around 209,000 m³/s — about 20% of all freshwater discharge into oceans globally.

Hydrographs plot discharge against time. The lag time between peak rainfall and peak discharge tells you about basin response — flashy (urban) vs. slow (forested, with infiltration).

Gauging stations are operated by the Environment Agency in England and the USGS in the US.
items.why: Units carry meaning. Discharge is a flow rate (volume/time), not a level (depth) — confusing these is the most common student error and undermines flood-frequency understanding.

items.title: Around 85% of the Nile's flow comes from Ethiopia
items.claim: Where does most of the Nile's water originate?

options.text: Lake Victoria provides most of the discharge
The Blue Nile (rising at Lake Tana in Ethiopia) and the Atbara — both fed by monsoonal rains in the Ethiopian Highlands — together provide around 85% of the Nile's annual discharge
Groundwater seepage in Sudan
Rainfall directly on Egypt

items.reveal:
The White Nile drains the East African plateau and Lake Victoria but loses much to evaporation in the Sudd swamps. Its contribution to the lower Nile is around 15-30%.

The Blue Nile rises from Lake Tana and falls steeply through the Ethiopian Highlands, fed by the Indian Ocean monsoon between June and September. The Atbara contributes additional seasonal flow.

The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), filling since 2020, has triggered serious dispute with Egypt and Sudan precisely because it controls the dominant source.
items.why: Water politics in the Nile basin is geographically determined by where the water comes from. The 1929 and 1959 treaties allocated Egypt and Sudan most of the flow — without Ethiopia, the source country.

items.title: The 1931 Yangtze flood killed millions
items.claim: What was the death toll of the 1931 China floods?

options.text: Around 100,000 — comparable to other major river floods
Estimates range from 422,000 to over 4 million dead — likely the deadliest natural disaster of the 20th century
Around 50 — minor in human terms
No reliable estimate exists

items.reveal:
The 1931 floods affected the Yangtze, Huai and Yellow river basins after extreme monsoon rainfall. Chris Courtney's 'The Nature of Disaster in China' (2018) places direct deaths from drowning at around 150,000 and total deaths including disease and famine at perhaps 2 million; older estimates went higher.

Wuhan was submerged for weeks. The Republic of China government's response was overwhelmed by the simultaneous Mukden Incident (September 1931, Japanese invasion of Manchuria).
items.why: River flooding remains the deadliest natural hazard category by long-term death toll. Vulnerability is not just about hazard — it's about state capacity, infrastructure and political moment.

items.title: Meanders migrate downstream over time
items.claim: What happens to meanders over years to decades?

options.text: They are fixed features that maintain their shape
Erosion on the outer bank and deposition on the inner bank cause meanders to migrate downstream and laterally, eventually being cut off as oxbow lakes
Meanders only form in glacial rivers
They migrate upstream against the current

items.reveal:
Helical flow concentrates velocity on the outer bend (river cliff, undercut) and slows it on the inner bend (point bar, deposition). The thalweg (line of fastest flow) traces an S-curve.

Mississippi meander cutoffs were mapped by Harold Fisk for the US Army Corps of Engineers in 1944 — showing the river's channel migrating across tens of kilometres of floodplain over centuries. The Corps now actively manages cutoffs.

Oxbow lakes form when erosion narrows a meander neck until the river breaks through and abandons the loop.
items.why: Floodplains are dynamic. Property and infrastructure built across meandering rivers face migration as well as flooding hazards — a slower but inevitable risk.

items.title: Sea level is rising 3-4 mm per year and accelerating
items.claim: How fast is global mean sea level rising?

options.text: It has been stable for centuries
Satellite altimetry since 1993 shows around 3.4 mm/year average, with the rate accelerating since 2010; IPCC AR6 projects 0.3-1.0 m rise by 2100 depending on emissions
Around 10 cm per year
Sea level is falling globally

items.reveal:
Thermal expansion of warming ocean water contributes about 40% of recent rise; melt from glaciers and ice sheets the rest. Greenland's mass loss has accelerated from around 50 Gt/year in the 1990s to around 280 Gt/year by 2010s (NASA GRACE data).

Local sea-level rise differs from global. Isostatic rebound (Scotland rising, southern England sinking) and ocean dynamic processes mean some coasts experience faster relative rise.

The AMOC slowdown could redistribute Atlantic sea level — raising it on the US East Coast more than the average.
items.why: Sea-level rise is not uniform and not linear. Local coastal management must plan against regional projections, not a single global figure.

items.title: Hard sea defences cause 'coastal squeeze'
items.claim: What is 'coastal squeeze'?

options.text: When two coastlines compete for tourism
When rising sea levels meet fixed hard defences (sea walls), intertidal habitats (saltmarsh, mudflat) cannot migrate inland and are progressively lost
Compression of coastal rocks by tides
Increased coastal traffic in summer

items.reveal_title: Habitat caught between rising sea and hard walls
items.reveal:
Saltmarshes and mudflats are critical for biodiversity, wave attenuation and carbon storage. They normally migrate inland as sea level rises — but cannot if blocked by sea walls.

Managed realignment (e.g. Wallasea Island, Essex, 2015) deliberately breaches old walls to allow habitat to re-form inland. The Environment Agency now uses Shoreline Management Plans with options including 'no active intervention', 'managed realignment' and 'hold the line'.

The Netherlands' Room for the River programme (2007-2018) is a related continental example.
items.why: Hard engineering has a long-term ecological cost. Coastal management policy is increasingly about choosing where to defend, where to retreat, and accepting losses elsewhere.

items.title: The English Channel is not getting narrower
items.claim: Is the English Channel closing as Britain and France converge?

options.text: Yes, by about 1 cm per year
No — there is no convergent plate boundary; both sit on the Eurasian plate. The Channel was carved by megaflood erosion around 450,000 and 160,000 years ago
Yes, by about 1 metre per year
It widens by 10 cm per year

items.reveal:
Britain was connected to mainland Europe as recently as 8,000 years ago (the Doggerland landscape). The Channel itself was formed by catastrophic megafloods when a glacial lake in the southern North Sea breached a chalk ridge at Dover-Calais (Gupta et al., Nature 2007).

Both Britain and France sit on the Eurasian plate, with no relative motion at this scale. The 'closing' or 'opening' claim is geophysically wrong.

Isostatic rebound is causing northern Britain to rise and southern England to sink — relative sea level rises faster on the south coast.
items.why: Plausible-sounding numerical claims about geographic change can be entirely fictional. The right test is mechanism, not vivid number — there's no plate boundary to drive Channel closure.

items.title: Longshore drift can move entire beaches kilometres
items.claim: What does longshore drift do?

options.text: It moves sand offshore into deep water
Wave-driven net sediment transport along the coast in the direction of prevailing waves — building spits (Spurn, Dawlish Warren) and stripping beaches downdrift of groynes
It mixes salt and freshwater at estuaries
It transports sediment upstream in rivers

items.reveal:
Swash hits the beach at an angle (the angle of incoming waves) and backwash returns straight downslope under gravity. Net effect: sediment moves along the coast, often metres per day for fine sand.

Spurn Head (Yorkshire) is a 5 km spit built by longshore drift carrying sediment from Holderness cliffs (eroding at up to 2 m/year) southward. The cliffs supply around 1 million m³ of sediment per year.

Groynes trap drift on their up-drift side and starve beaches on the down-drift side — a coastal management trade-off.
items.why: Coastal protection in one place can damage another. Sediment budgets are zero-sum: a beach kept by groynes is sand denied to the next beach down the coast.

items.title: Spring tides happen at full and new moon — twice a month
items.claim: What causes spring tides (the largest tidal range)?

options.text: Spring tides only happen in March-April (the spring season)
When Sun, Earth and Moon align (at full and new moon), solar and lunar tidal pulls combine — happening roughly every 14 days, regardless of season
Only the Sun affects tides
Spring tides occur once a year at the equinox

items.reveal:
The Moon provides about two-thirds of the tidal force; the Sun about one-third. At new and full moon (syzygy), the bodies align and the bulges add — spring tides. At first and last quarter, they are at 90° — neap tides, smaller.

The Bristol Channel has the second-highest tidal range in the world (around 15 m at Avonmouth). The Bay of Fundy (Canada) tops it at around 16 m. Severn Bore tides on the spring tide can reach 2 m as a wave.

'Spring' here comes from Old English 'springan' — to leap or rise — not from the season.
items.why: Etymological confusion turns into scientific confusion. The Moon's role is obvious but the Sun's contribution and the geometric reason for the fortnightly cycle are often missed.

items.title: Most of Britain was under ice 20,000 years ago
items.claim: How much of the UK was covered by ice at the Last Glacial Maximum?

options.text: None — Britain has never been glaciated
Most of the country north of the Thames was under ice up to around 1 km thick at the LGM (around 20,000 years ago), with southern England as a permafrost tundra zone
Only the Scottish Highlands were glaciated
All of the UK was under permanent ice until 1500 CE

items.reveal:
The British-Irish Ice Sheet extended to roughly the Thames-Severn line. Ice was up to 1 km thick over the Highlands. Glacial landforms — corries (Snowdonia, Lake District), U-shaped valleys (Glencoe), drumlins (Eden Valley) and erratics (Norber, Yorkshire) — record the maximum.

The Younger Dryas (around 12,900-11,700 years ago) was a final cold snap with small Highland glaciers (the Loch Lomond Stadial). Britain became ice-free by around 10,000 years ago.

Britain rejoined Europe geographically about 8,200 years ago when the Storegga submarine landslide tsunami finished off Doggerland.
items.why: Most British landforms are products of the Ice Ages, not earlier processes. The shape of the country is recent and contingent.

items.title: Scotland is still rising — England is sinking
items.claim: What is happening to the British Isles vertically due to glacial isostatic adjustment?

options.text: Both are stable — Britain has fully recovered from the last Ice Age
Scotland and northern England rise by 1-2 mm/year as crust rebounds from glacial loading; southern and eastern England sink by around 1 mm/year
All of Britain is sinking equally
The British Isles tilt is not measurable

items.reveal:
When the last ice sheet melted (about 10,000 years ago), the depressed crust began to rise. The mantle's slow viscous flow means rebound is still happening. GPS networks (BIGF, the British Isles GNSS Facilities) measure the motion directly.

Net result for relative sea level: southern England experiences faster sea-level rise than would be expected from climate alone, while northern Scotland experiences slower (or even falling) relative sea level. This is one reason why Thames and Hull tidal defences face accelerating pressure.

Fenno-Scandinavia is rising even faster (10 mm/year in parts of the Gulf of Bothnia).
items.why: Climate-change sea-level projections must be combined with local geophysics. A coast is rising or sinking on its own terms, and the climate signal sits on top of that.

items.title: Glaciers move metres to hundreds of metres per year
items.claim: How fast does ice in a typical valley glacier move?

options.text: Around 1 km per year for all glaciers
Typically tens to hundreds of metres per year, with surge events reaching kilometres per year. Greenland's Jakobshavn glacier reached around 17 km/year in 2012
Glaciers are stationary — only the snow at the top moves
About 1 mm per year — too slow to measure

items.reveal:
Glacier motion has two components: internal deformation (ice flowing under its own weight, around 10-100 m/year for valley glaciers) and basal sliding (much faster when meltwater lubricates the bed).

Surge-type glaciers (about 1% of glaciers) accelerate by an order of magnitude for months or years. Variegated Glacier (Alaska, 1982-83) surged at 65 m/day. Jakobshavn Isbrae (Greenland) is one of the fastest, sometimes called the source of the iceberg that sank Titanic.

Climate warming has accelerated outlet glaciers in Greenland and Antarctica as ice shelves break up and remove buttressing.
items.why: Glacier dynamics control how fast ice sheets contribute to sea level. Understanding flow speeds — and acceleration mechanisms — is central to projecting future sea-level rise.

items.title: Antarctica and Greenland are losing hundreds of gigatonnes of ice per year
items.claim: How much ice is being lost from the polar ice sheets?

options.text: Negligible — both ice sheets are stable
Greenland: around 280 Gt/year (2010s average); Antarctica: around 150 Gt/year, accelerating, largely from West Antarctic outlet glaciers like Pine Island and Thwaites
Antarctica is gaining ice while Greenland loses
Both are losing around 10,000 Gt/year — much faster than reported

items.reveal:
NASA's GRACE satellites (2002-2017) and GRACE-FO (since 2018) measure ice mass directly via the gravity changes it causes. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change AR6 (2021) and the IMBIE Team's 2018 and 2020 reconciliations of multiple methods are the standard references.

1 mm of global sea-level rise requires about 360 Gt of ice melt. Current ice-sheet loss contributes around 1 mm/year — about a third of total sea-level rise.

Thwaites Glacier (the 'Doomsday Glacier') alone could raise global sea level by around 65 cm if it collapsed.
items.why: Ice sheets are the largest reservoirs of freshwater on Earth. Their stability — or instability — is one of the largest uncertainties in long-term climate projections.

items.title: The Gulf Stream keeps the UK warmer than it would otherwise be
items.claim: How much does the Gulf Stream warm Britain?

options.text: Not at all — UK climate is determined by latitude alone
Comparison with similar-latitude locations (Calgary, Labrador) suggests the wider North Atlantic Current warms western Europe by around 5-10°C above what latitude would predict
By around 30°C — without it Britain would be like Antarctica
By less than 0.1°C

items.reveal:
The Gulf Stream is the western boundary current of the North Atlantic gyre; it widens north of Cape Hatteras into the North Atlantic Current. Prevailing westerlies carry the warm air onto western Europe.

Richard Seager and colleagues (2002) argued that latitude differences and atmospheric heat transport from west to east are at least as important as the ocean current itself. The popular 'Gulf Stream alone keeps Britain warm' line oversimplifies.

The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) has weakened by an estimated 15% since the mid-20th century (Caesar et al., 2018, 2021).
items.why: Climate is the product of multiple systems. Single-cause stories (it's the Gulf Stream!) miss how ocean and atmosphere together shape regional temperature.

items.title: The jet stream sits around 10 km above the surface
items.claim: What is the jet stream?

options.text: A surface wind near the equator
A narrow band of fast westerly winds (often 100-300 km/h) at around 9-12 km altitude (the tropopause), driven by temperature contrasts between polar and tropical air masses
An ocean current in the Pacific
A jet of supersonic air over deserts

items.reveal:
The polar jet (UK weather) and subtropical jet are the major Northern Hemisphere features. They meander in Rossby waves, and the shape of those waves controls where storm systems track.

Jet streams were discovered by Japanese balloon-bombing campaigns of WWII and by US bomber crews over the Pacific (1944) flying west into apparently impossible headwinds.

Arctic amplification (warming of the Arctic at roughly 4x the global rate) reduces the temperature contrast that drives the polar jet, possibly causing it to meander more — linked to more persistent weather extremes.
items.why: Surface weather has upper-atmosphere causes. Understanding why summer 2022 had heat domes or 2013-14 had stuck storm tracks requires looking at the jet.

items.title: The Arctic is warming around 4 times faster than the global average
items.claim: What is 'Arctic amplification'?

options.text: A myth — the Arctic warms at the same rate as the tropics
The Arctic has warmed approximately 4 times the global mean since 1979, driven by ice-albedo feedback, water-vapour feedback and changes in heat transport
The Arctic is cooling
It is amplification only in winter

items.reveal:
Mika Rantanen and colleagues (Nature Communications Earth & Environment, 2022) revised the figure from a long-cited 2x to nearly 4x for the Arctic Circle since 1979.

Ice-albedo feedback: white ice reflects around 80% of solar radiation; open ocean absorbs around 90%. As sea ice retreats, more energy is absorbed. Arctic sea ice extent in September has fallen from around 7 million km² (1979) to under 4 million km² (recent minima).

Downstream effects: ocean stratification, changes in jet stream, methane release from thawing permafrost.
items.why: Average warming hides extreme regional warming. The Arctic case shows how feedbacks can multiply the local signal — and why polar regions are decisive for global climate trajectory.

items.title: El Nino and La Nina drive global climate every 2-7 years
items.claim: What is the El Nino-Southern Oscillation (ENSO)?

options.text: A single storm in the Pacific
A coupled ocean-atmosphere oscillation in the tropical Pacific that occurs every 2-7 years; El Nino (warm phase) and La Nina (cool phase) reshape global rainfall, drought and storm patterns
An Atlantic ocean current
An annual cycle in the Arctic

items.reveal:
El Nino: warming of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, weakened trade winds, shifted convection. Effects include drought in Australia, Indonesia and South Africa; floods in Peru, Ecuador and east Africa; weaker Atlantic hurricane season.

La Nina: opposite phase. The 1997-98 El Nino was among the strongest; 2015-16 caused mass coral bleaching on the Great Barrier Reef and contributed to record global temperatures.

Gilbert Walker first identified the 'Southern Oscillation' atmospheric pattern in 1924 from Indian Meteorological Department records.
items.why: Global weather is partly oscillatory. Forecasts months ahead become more skilful when ENSO state is known — and crops, water supplies and disaster planning in many countries depend on the call.

items.title: The Indian monsoon is driven by land-sea temperature contrast
items.claim: What causes the South Asian summer monsoon?

options.text: Earth's tilt alone
Differential heating: in summer, the Asian continent heats up faster than the Indian Ocean, creating a low-pressure zone that draws in moist oceanic air, reversed in winter
Tropical cyclones combining each year
The Earth's gravitational interaction with the Moon

items.reveal:
From June to September, the Tibetan Plateau heats intensely; low-level winds reverse and blow from southwest, bringing moisture from the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal. The Indian subcontinent receives perhaps 80% of its annual rainfall in these months.

The Himalayas force orographic lifting, producing the wettest places on Earth (Mawsynram, Cherrapunji — Meghalaya). The Western Ghats also lift the air.

Climate change is shifting monsoon onset and intensity. The Indian Meteorological Department's date of onset has varied by weeks in recent decades. Around 1.5 billion people depend on the monsoon for agriculture.
items.why: Monsoon variability is one of the highest-stakes climate signals on Earth. A failed monsoon means famine; a strong one means floods. The mechanism (differential heating) is testable physics — but its variability is poorly forecast.

items.title: The Amazon transpires its own rainfall
items.claim: How important is Amazon vegetation to its own rainfall?

options.text: Rainfall comes entirely from the Atlantic; vegetation is irrelevant
Trees transpire huge quantities of water vapour, generating 'flying rivers' that recycle moisture 5-6 times across the basin and supply rainfall to southeast South America
Rainfall is driven by Andean snowmelt
There is no rainfall in the Amazon

items.reveal:
A mature Amazon tree can transpire 200-1,000 litres a day. Antonio Nobre's 'flying rivers' concept (popularised through INPE Brazilian space agency research) describes the moisture flux from the basin to the south, equivalent to or greater than the Amazon River's discharge.

Deforestation reduces transpiration; some regions of the southern and eastern Amazon are already net carbon sources (Gatti et al., Nature 2021). A tipping point at perhaps 20-25% deforestation could shift large parts of the forest to savannah, with knock-on effects on Brazilian agriculture.
items.why: Forests are climate machines, not passive vegetation cover. The Amazon's ecological role is hydrological as much as biological — and its loss would change rainfall patterns far outside the basin.

items.title: Rainforest soils are mostly nutrient-poor
items.claim: What is the surprising fact about tropical rainforest soils?

options.text: They are deep, dark and extremely fertile
Most are highly weathered, leached and nutrient-poor — the biomass holds most nutrients, which are rapidly recycled through the litter layer
They are largely sand and contain no organic matter
They contain unusually high mineral content from volcanism

items.reveal_title: Fertility in the trees, not the ground
items.reveal:
Heavy rainfall leaches soluble nutrients from tropical soils, leaving iron- and aluminium-rich red oxisols (latosols). Decomposition is rapid in heat and moisture; nutrients are immediately re-absorbed by shallow root mats and mycorrhizal networks.

Amazonian 'terra preta' soils are a notable exception — black earths created by pre-Columbian populations using charcoal, bone and waste, persisting for centuries and now studied as a biochar model.

Slash-and-burn agriculture works for 2-3 years before fertility crashes, because the burn temporarily releases nutrients held in vegetation.
items.why: Lush vegetation does not imply rich soil. The fertility myth has driven destructive agricultural expansion into rainforests for centuries — and explains why cleared land often degrades quickly.

items.title: Coral reefs cover under 1% of the ocean but host around 25% of marine species
items.claim: What proportion of marine biodiversity do coral reefs support?

options.text: Less than 1%
Around 25% of all marine species live on coral reefs, which cover less than 1% of the ocean floor — perhaps the most concentrated biodiversity hotspot on Earth
About 75%
Coral reefs support only the species visible to divers

items.reveal:
Reefs occupy around 284,000 km² globally — under 0.1% of the ocean. The Great Barrier Reef is 2,300 km long. Species counts: around 4,000 fish species, 800 reef-building coral species, plus uncounted invertebrates.

Mass bleaching events (1998, 2010, 2014-17, 2024) have hit major reef systems. The Great Barrier Reef has experienced bleaching in 2016, 2017, 2020, 2022 and 2024. Some 50% of shallow corals on the GBR died in the 2016 event.

Reefs also provide coastal protection, fisheries and tourism value estimated at hundreds of billions of dollars annually.
items.why: Conservation priorities follow concentration. A small fraction of the planet holds an outsized share of biodiversity — losing reefs means losing whole ecosystems, not just iconic species.

items.title: The oceans absorb more CO2 than all forests combined
items.claim: Which is the larger annual carbon sink?

options.text: Forests, by a wide margin
Oceans absorb around 25% of anthropogenic CO2 (around 2.5 GtC/year); land sinks (mainly forests) take up around 31%, but oceans hold by far the larger total reservoir
Neither — CO2 stays in the atmosphere
Glaciers absorb most CO2

items.reveal:
Global Carbon Project annual budget: of around 10 GtC/year emitted by humans, around 25% goes to oceans, around 31% to land, and around 44% remains in the atmosphere (where it has driven the CO2 rise from 280 ppm pre-industrial to over 420 ppm).

Oceans absorb CO2 by both physical (cold water absorbing more) and biological (phytoplankton fixing carbon) pathways. The result is ocean acidification — pH has fallen by around 0.1 since pre-industrial, a 30% increase in H+ concentration.

Deforestation is itself a major source of CO2, partly offsetting the land sink.
items.why: Climate accounting is about budgets. Both sinks are essential — and both are at risk: ocean uptake is slowing as warming reduces solubility; land uptake is stressed by drought and fire.

items.title: 36 biodiversity hotspots hold around 50% of plant species
items.claim: What is a 'biodiversity hotspot'?

options.text: Any tropical area
Regions with at least 1,500 endemic vascular plants and at least 70% original habitat loss — 36 defined globally by Conservation International, holding around 50% of plants and 43% of vertebrates
Any island over 100 km²
Only the Amazon and Congo basins

items.reveal:
Norman Myers identified the concept in 1988; Conservation International refined it. The 36 hotspots include Madagascar, the Atlantic Forest of Brazil, the Mediterranean Basin, the California Floristic Province, Sundaland, and more.

Total hotspot area is now about 2.4% of Earth's land surface — and yet holds the indicated share of species. Original extents were around 16% of land surface; the rest has been lost to human use.

IUCN Red List, BirdLife International's Important Bird Areas and the Alliance for Zero Extinction overlay related conservation priority maps.
items.why: Conservation cannot save every place. Hotspot prioritisation is one — contested — way of allocating effort to where it can save the most species. The trade-off with savanna, boreal and ocean priorities is real.

items.title: There are now over 30 megacities globally
items.claim: How many megacities (over 10 million inhabitants) currently exist?

options.text: Around 5 — all in the developed world
Around 33 megacities as of 2022 (UN), with Tokyo the largest at around 37 million; most are in Asia and the Global South
Around 100, distributed evenly globally
Only Tokyo qualifies

items.reveal:
UN World Urbanization Prospects (2018, updated 2022): 33 cities exceed 10 million. Largest: Tokyo (37 m), Delhi (32 m), Shanghai (28 m), Dhaka (23 m), São Paulo (22 m), Cairo (22 m), Mexico City (22 m), Beijing (21 m), Mumbai (21 m).

Lagos (Nigeria, around 15 m) is growing fastest; UN projects it could pass 30 m by 2050. By 2050, the projection is around 50 megacities, most in Africa and South Asia.

Defining a 'city' is itself contested — metropolitan area, agglomeration, urban functional area all give different numbers.
items.why: The geography of global population is shifting. 19th-century urban hierarchies (London, New York, Paris) no longer describe reality. The major cities of the 21st century are largely in countries that were poor a generation ago.

items.title: Gentrification raises rents and displaces residents
items.claim: What is the core mechanism of gentrification?

options.text: Wealthy newcomers move into deprived neighbourhoods, raising rents and property prices, often displacing existing residents who can no longer afford to stay
Demolition of inner-city housing by the state alone
A spontaneous improvement in services without displacement
An exclusively positive process with no losers

items.reveal:
Ruth Glass coined the term in 1964 in 'London: Aspects of Change', describing changes in Islington. Neil Smith's 'rent gap' theory (1979) explains gentrification by the gap between actual and potential rent in disinvested areas.

London examples: Notting Hill (1960s onwards), Brixton (2000s onwards), Hackney (2000s). New York: SoHo, Williamsburg. Berlin: Prenzlauer Berg, Kreuzberg.

London now has displacement-mitigation policies (affordable housing quotas, right-to-return clauses on estate redevelopment), though their effectiveness is debated.
items.why: Urban regeneration creates both winners and losers. Glossy 'rejuvenation' narratives obscure the costs to displaced residents — and the question of who the city is being improved for.

items.title: Most workers in low-income countries are in the informal economy
items.claim: What share of employment is informal in LICs?

options.text: Under 10%
Around 90% of employment in low-income countries and around 60% globally is informal (ILO, 2018) — without formal contracts, social protection or tax registration
About 25% in all countries
Informal work is now extinct

items.reveal:
The International Labour Organization defines informal employment as work without legal recognition or social protection. The estimate is around 2 billion workers globally, with concentrations in sub-Saharan Africa (around 89% of non-agricultural employment) and South Asia (around 86%).

Key activities: street vending, waste picking, domestic work, small-scale agriculture. Many informal workers are women.

The term came from Keith Hart's 1971 fieldwork in Accra, Ghana. The ILO has worked since 2015 (Recommendation 204) on transitioning workers to the formal economy.
items.why: Models of 'employment' built on the Global North get developing-world economies wrong. The informal sector is not marginal — it is the modal experience of work for billions.

items.title: GDP per capita misses much of what makes a country 'developed'
items.claim: Why is the Human Development Index (HDI) sometimes preferred to GDP per capita?

options.text: GDP per capita is the only useful measure
HDI (created 1990 by Mahbub ul Haq and Amartya Sen) combines life expectancy, education and GNI per capita — capturing health and education outcomes that GDP misses
HDI measures government spending only
HDI replaces all economic statistics

items.reveal:
HDI uses three components: life expectancy at birth, expected and mean years of schooling, and GNI per capita (PPP). Each is normalised between 0 and 1 and combined as a geometric mean.

2022 HDI rankings: Switzerland (1), Norway (2), Iceland (3); UK (15); US (21). Niger, South Sudan and Somalia at the bottom. The Inequality-adjusted HDI (IHDI) adjusts for inequality within countries — the US falls further in the IHDI than the UK or Germany.

The UN now also tracks the Gender Inequality Index (GII), the Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) and the Sustainable Development Goal indicators.
items.why: What gets measured shapes priorities. A country with a high HDI is not just rich but has converted wealth into health and education — a meaningfully different policy success.

items.title: The Brandt Line is now badly outdated
items.claim: What is the Brandt Line and why is it controversial?

options.text: A current political boundary still in active use

A line drawn on a 1980 report by Willy Brandt dividing the world's rich North from the poor South — but it places South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore, the UAE and Saudi Arabia in the 'South' despite high incomes
A natural climatic boundary at the Tropic of Cancer
An EU policy boundary

items.reveal:
The Brandt Commission's report 'North-South: A Programme for Survival' (1980) divided the world by a line dipping south to include Australia and New Zealand in the rich 'North'.

Since then: South Korea's GDP per capita has risen from around $1,700 (1980) to over $34,000 (2022). China's has risen from $300 to $12,500. The Gulf states have grown dramatically. Meanwhile parts of southern and eastern Europe have stagnated.

Alternative frameworks: World Bank country income classifications (low / lower-middle / upper-middle / high), the UN's Least Developed Country list, the BRICS grouping. The 'Global South' as a political-solidarity category is now distinct from the original geographical line.
items.why: Categories age. Using a 1980 division to describe the 2020s misses 40 years of differential development — and can lead to lazy assumptions about which countries are rich or poor.

items.title: Choropleth maps show areal data; isoline maps show continuous data
items.claim: What is the difference between a choropleth and an isoline map?

options.text: There is no difference — they are alternative names for the same thing
Choropleth: areas (countries, counties) shaded by category. Isoline (or isarithmic): lines connecting points of equal value (contours, isobars, isotherms)
Choropleth maps show only relief
Isoline maps cannot show climate data

items.reveal:
Choropleth maps assume relatively uniform values within each area. They are vulnerable to the Modifiable Areal Unit Problem (MAUP) — different boundary choices produce different patterns.

Isoline maps treat the variable as a continuous surface. Examples: contour lines (relief), isobars (atmospheric pressure), isotherms (temperature), isohyets (rainfall).

Dot maps, proportional symbols, flow lines and cartograms are other techniques. The choice of map type encodes assumptions about how the data behaves spatially.
items.why: Map technique matters. The same data, mapped differently, tells different stories — and the right technique depends on whether the variable is areal or continuous in nature.

items.title: A 4-figure grid reference is precise to 1 km; a 6-figure to 100 m
items.claim: What precision does each give on a UK Ordnance Survey map?

options.text: Both refer to a point
4-figure references identify a 1 km × 1 km square; 6-figure references identify a 100 m × 100 m square. 8-figure references give 10 m precision
4-figure is more precise than 6-figure
References are accurate to 1 metre regardless

items.reveal:
OS uses a National Grid: read eastings (left-right) first, then northings (bottom-up). 'Along the corridor, then up the stairs.'

Grid letters (SE, NY etc.) identify 100 km squares. A full reference combines letters with numerical eastings/northings — e.g. SE 5436 (4-figure within the SE square, locating a 1 km grid square; SE 543 367 for 6-figure 100 m precision).

The National Grid covers Great Britain only; Northern Ireland uses the Irish Grid. GPS coordinates (latitude/longitude or UTM) are international alternatives.
items.why: Map references are not arbitrary precision. Reporting weather or accident locations using inconsistent precision causes real navigation failures — including search-and-rescue.

items.title: Correlation does not imply causation
items.claim: What does a Spearman's rank correlation coefficient measure?

options.text: Whether one variable causes another
The strength and direction of monotonic association between ranked variables, between -1 (perfect negative) and +1 (perfect positive); 0 indicates no monotonic relationship
The mean of the two variables
Only the strength of a linear relationship

items.reveal:
Spearman's ρ uses ranks rather than raw values, making it robust to outliers and non-linear monotonic relationships. Pearson's r requires linear relationship and normally-distributed data.

Critical values must be checked against sample size: with n=10, ρ must exceed about 0.564 to be significant at p=0.05. With n=30, the threshold falls to around 0.306.

A strong correlation can be coincidental (ice cream sales and drownings — both rise in summer), confounded by a third variable, or even reversed in direction (Simpson's paradox).
items.why: Statistical reasoning is part of geographical skills. Strong correlation is evidence, not proof; geographers must always argue causation separately from association.

items.title: Sampling strategy affects every fieldwork result
items.claim: Why does a geographer choose a stratified sample over a random one?

options.text: It is always quicker
Stratified sampling deliberately includes proportions from defined subgroups (e.g. age categories in a questionnaire, river sections by gradient), reducing risk of missing minority categories
It produces fewer data points
It cannot be statistically analysed

items.reveal:
Sampling types: random (every member equally likely), systematic (every nth member, e.g. every 10 metres along a transect), stratified (proportional samples from defined groups), opportunistic (whoever is available — least rigorous).

At A-level, the NEA Independent Investigation requires explicit justification of sampling strategy. Small samples (n<30) limit statistical analysis; sub-group analysis needs larger samples in each stratum.

Fieldwork ethics, including consent for questionnaires and impact on study sites, has become more prominent.
items.why: Bad sampling produces bad results regardless of how impressive the spreadsheet looks. Sampling design is upstream of all subsequent analysis.

items.title: OS map symbols are standardised across the country
items.claim: What do contour lines on an OS map show?

options.text: Roads and paths
Lines connecting points of equal elevation above sea level — closer contours indicate steeper slopes; index contours (heavier lines) are typically every 50 m on 1:50,000 maps
Property boundaries
The route of the prime meridian

items.reveal:
OS 1:50,000 Landranger maps have contour intervals of 10 m in lowlands and 5 m in some upland areas. 1:25,000 Explorer maps have 5 or 10 m contours.

Closed loop contours with the highest values inside indicate a hill summit. V-shaped contours pointing uphill indicate river valleys. Cliffs are shown by hachures or special symbols.

Key symbols: black for human features (roads, buildings, boundaries), blue for water, brown for relief, green for vegetation.
items.why: Map literacy is a portable geographical skill. Whether reading for navigation, fieldwork or planning, the visual grammar of OS maps depends on understanding contour interval and symbol conventions.

items.title: Cities are 2-10 °C warmer than surrounding countryside
items.claim: What is the urban heat island (UHI) effect?

options.text: A myth — cities are no warmer than rural areas
Cities are typically 2-5 °C warmer than surrounding rural areas (up to 10 °C in extreme cases at night) due to dark surfaces, reduced evapotranspiration, anthropogenic heat and reduced sky view
Cities are colder than countryside due to shade
Only New York shows the effect

items.reveal:
Causes of UHI: dark asphalt and concrete have low albedo (absorb solar radiation); reduced vegetation cuts evaporative cooling; tall buildings trap re-emitted infrared (sky-view factor); waste heat from vehicles and air conditioning; thermal mass releases heat at night.

London during the 2003 heatwave was around 4-9 °C warmer than surrounding countryside at night. UHI contributed to the death toll (around 2,000 excess deaths in the UK).

Mitigation: green roofs, urban trees, light-coloured surfaces, water features, ventilation corridors in city planning.
items.why: Urban climate is human-made microclimate. Climate change interacts with UHI to make heatwaves more dangerous in cities — a fast-rising public health hazard.

items.title: Fold mountains form at convergent plate boundaries
items.claim: How do the Himalayas form?

options.text: By volcanic eruption
By the collision of the Indian and Eurasian continental plates, ongoing for around 50 million years and still uplifting at 5-10 mm/year
By erosion of a high plateau
By isostatic rebound from glacial retreat

items.reveal:
The Indian plate moved north at 15-20 cm/year through the Cenozoic — fast enough that the closure of the Tethys Ocean and collision with Eurasia produced the highest mountains on Earth.

Other active fold mountain systems: the Alps (Africa-Europe collision), the Andes (oceanic-continental subduction), the Caucasus, the Atlas. Older eroded systems: the Appalachians, the Caledonides (Scotland), the Urals.

India continues to push north at around 5 cm/year, still uplifting the Himalayas — and triggering many of the world's largest earthquakes along the Main Frontal Thrust.
items.why: Mountain building is active geology. The Himalayas are not static features but a still-unfolding consequence of plate motion — and the cause of regional seismic hazard.

items.title: Rural-urban migration is mostly young adults
items.claim: Who migrates from rural areas to cities in low- and middle-income countries?

options.text: Whole families move together as a single unit

Predominantly young adults (15-35) seeking employment, with selective patterns by gender — some societies see male-dominated industrial migration, others (e.g. textiles in Bangladesh, domestic work in the Philippines) see female-dominated
Elderly people seek better healthcare in cities
Migration is randomly distributed across all age groups

items.reveal:
Selective migration reshapes both source (ageing populations, women-headed households where men migrate, remittance economies) and destination (skewed urban demographics, housing pressure).

Mexico-US migration is largely male; Filipina overseas workers are mostly women. Bangladesh garment-industry urban migration is around 80% female. Pacific Island remittance dependence is heavy.

Remittances to LICs and MICs reached around $640 billion in 2022 (World Bank) — more than total foreign direct investment to many countries.
items.why: Migration is age- and gender-selective in ways that reshape entire economies. Treating migration as a uniform mass misses the demographic specifics that drive both impacts and policy.

items.title: Most fresh water on Earth is locked in ice
items.claim: Where is most of Earth's freshwater?

options.text: Mostly in rivers and lakes
Around 68% of freshwater is in glaciers and ice caps; around 30% is groundwater; surface water (rivers, lakes, wetlands) is under 1% of freshwater and about 0.01% of all water on Earth
Mainly in the atmosphere
Mostly in the oceans

items.reveal:
Earth's total water: around 97.5% saline (oceans), 2.5% fresh. Of that 2.5%: glaciers and ice caps around 68%, groundwater around 30%, surface and atmospheric water under 2%.

Groundwater is the world's largest accessible freshwater store but is being depleted in many regions (the Ogallala Aquifer, the North China Plain, parts of India). NASA GRACE satellites have mapped the depletion.

The Aral Sea, once the world's fourth-largest lake (68,000 km²), shrank by 90% from 1960 by Soviet irrigation diversions — one of the most visible water-management failures of the 20th century.
items.why: Water scarcity is partly a storage problem. Most freshwater is inaccessible (ice, deep aquifers); we depend on a tiny fraction — surface water and shallow aquifers — that is unevenly distributed and vulnerable.

items.title: Tropical cyclones need 26.5 °C sea surface temperatures
items.claim: What conditions are required for tropical cyclone formation?

options.text: Any warm region with rain
Sea surface temperatures of at least around 26.5 °C, low vertical wind shear, sufficient distance from the equator (Coriolis force) and a pre-existing disturbance — typically 5-30° latitude
Polar regions only
Land-only conditions

items.reveal:
Energy source: latent heat released as water vapour condenses. Tropical cyclones do not form within about 5° of the equator (insufficient Coriolis force to spin) and weaken rapidly over land or cool water.

Naming conventions: Atlantic/East Pacific = hurricanes; Northwest Pacific = typhoons; South Pacific/Indian Ocean = cyclones. Same phenomenon. The Saffir-Simpson scale (Category 1-5) classifies Atlantic and East Pacific storms by sustained wind speed.

Storm surge — wind-driven raising of sea level along the coast — is usually the deadliest hazard (Hurricane Katrina, 2005; Cyclone Bhola, 1970, killed at least 300,000 in East Pakistan).
items.why: Climate change is raising sea surface temperatures and expanding the zone where tropical cyclones can form and intensify. The deadliest hazard is also rising as warmer air holds more moisture.

items.title: Around 10 million hectares of forest are lost each year
items.claim: How much forest does the world lose annually?

options.text: Forest cover is increasing globally

Net loss is around 4.7 million hectares per year (FAO 2020), with gross tropical deforestation of around 10 million ha/year partly offset by plantation expansion and natural regeneration in temperate regions
Around 100 million hectares lost per year
Loss is confined to Brazil

items.reveal_title: Gross loss, net loss, and what counts
items.reveal:
FAO Global Forest Resources Assessment 2020: net forest loss of 4.7 million ha/year for 2010-2020, down from 7.8 million ha/year for 1990-2000. Tropical primary forest loss in 2022: around 4.1 million ha (Global Forest Watch).

Main drivers: cattle ranching (Amazon), palm oil (Indonesia, Malaysia), soybean expansion (Cerrado), small-holder agriculture (Congo Basin).

The distinction between primary forest and plantation matters: a monoculture plantation is not biodiverse forest, but counts as 'forest area' under FAO definitions.
items.why: Definitions shape the apparent crisis. 'Forest cover stable' can mean primary forest replaced by plantation. Following the right metric (intact primary forest, biodiversity) is essential to understand the real loss.

items.title: The 17 SDGs replaced the 8 Millennium Development Goals in 2015
items.claim: What are the UN Sustainable Development Goals?

options.text: A binding international treaty signed by all nations
17 goals with 169 targets agreed by UN member states in September 2015, to be met by 2030 — covering poverty, education, climate, gender equality and others; non-binding but with national reporting
EU-only policy goals
Goals applying only to LICs

items.reveal:
The Millennium Development Goals (2000-2015, 8 goals, 21 targets) focused on poverty reduction in LICs. The SDGs (2015-2030, 17 goals, 169 targets) apply universally — HICs are also measured.

Progress is monitored through Voluntary National Reviews. The UN's annual SDG report tracks the 232 indicators. The COVID-19 pandemic reversed progress on several goals; the UN reports that the world is not on track for any of the 17 goals at projected 2030.

The SDGs replaced the MDGs partly because the latter were criticised for being designed by HICs for LICs without sufficient consultation.
items.why: The architecture of international development matters. Whether progress targets are set globally and how they are measured shapes national policy priorities — even when there is no enforcement mechanism.

items.title: Antarctica is governed by an international treaty
items.claim: Who owns Antarctica?

options.text: It is divided into national territories
The 1959 Antarctic Treaty froze territorial claims, demilitarised the continent and committed it to scientific cooperation; 56 countries are now parties
Russia owns most of it
It is divided between Argentina and Chile

items.reveal:
The original 12 signatories (1959) included the US, USSR, UK, Australia, France, Argentina and Chile. The treaty entered force in 1961. The Protocol on Environmental Protection (Madrid Protocol, 1991, in force 1998) prohibits mineral extraction.

Seven countries maintain dormant territorial claims (UK, Norway, France, Australia, New Zealand, Argentina, Chile). The US and Russia reserve the right to claim. Treaty parties operate around 70 year-round research stations.

The treaty is one of the most successful international agreements of the Cold War era — both superpowers wanted the demilitarisation to apply to the other.
items.why: Some territory remains explicitly outside the state system. Antarctica's governance shows what's possible when no major power has a strong sovereignty claim — but also illustrates how fragile such arrangements may be as resource interests grow.

items.title: The Ring of Fire is a 40,000 km horseshoe of subduction zones
items.claim: What is the Pacific Ring of Fire?

options.text: A single underwater volcano in Hawaii
A roughly horseshoe-shaped zone around the Pacific basin where multiple plate boundaries — mostly subduction — produce around 90% of the world's earthquakes and around 75% of active volcanoes
A pattern visible only from satellites
An area without seismic activity

items.reveal:
The Ring follows the boundaries of the Pacific Plate against the Eurasian, North American, Philippine, Cocos, Nazca and Australian plates. Major subduction zones include the Aleutian Trench, Japan Trench, Mariana Trench, Tonga Trench, Peru-Chile Trench.

Notable Ring events: 1960 Valdivia (Chile, M9.5, largest ever recorded); 1964 Great Alaska (M9.2); 2004 Sumatra-Andaman (M9.1); 2011 Tohoku (M9.0). Volcanoes include Mount St Helens (1980), Pinatubo (1991), Krakatoa (1883) and Tambora (1815).

The USGS tracks around 50 earthquakes per day globally; most are Ring-of-Fire events too small to feel.
items.why: Hazard distribution follows tectonic structure. Building codes in Tokyo, Anchorage, Santiago and Wellington are calibrated to subduction-zone physics — and the underlying geology dictates the risk profile of entire economies.

items.title: A tsunami can cross the Pacific in under 24 hours
items.claim: How fast does a tsunami travel in deep ocean?

options.text: Around 30 km/h, comparable to wind waves
Around 700-900 km/h in deep ocean (calculated as √(g × depth)) — jet airliner speed; the 1960 Chile tsunami reached Hawaii (10,000 km away) in about 15 hours and Japan in around 22 hours
The speed of sound in water (around 5,400 km/h)
A fixed 100 km/h regardless of depth

items.reveal:
Tsunami speed in open ocean depends on depth: at 4,000 m, around 700 km/h; in 50 m, around 80 km/h. As the wave shoals at coasts, energy compresses vertically and the wave grows from under a metre to potentially tens of metres.

The 1960 Chilean earthquake (M9.5) generated a Pacific-wide tsunami: Hawaii saw 10 m waves around 15 hours later; Japan, 17,000 km away, saw 5 m waves 22 hours after. 142 people died in Japan from a Chilean earthquake.

The Pacific Tsunami Warning Center (Honolulu, 1949) uses DART buoys (Deep-ocean Assessment and Reporting of Tsunamis) to detect pressure changes from passing waves.
items.why: Distance gives time for warning across ocean basins — but not for nearby coasts. The 2004 Sumatran tsunami killed locally in minutes; Sri Lanka had two hours; Somalia had seven. Warning systems must work at all timescales.

items.title: Eruption columns can punch 30-40 km into the stratosphere
items.claim: How high can volcanic eruption columns reach?

options.text: Limited to the lower troposphere (under 5 km)

Large Plinian eruptions can exceed 30-40 km — well into the stratosphere; Mount Pinatubo (1991) reached around 35 km, injecting sulphur dioxide that cooled global temperatures by around 0.5°C for 18 months
They never enter the stratosphere
Around 100 km, into space

items.reveal:
Plinian eruptions are named after Pliny the Younger's letters describing Vesuvius in 79 CE. Pinatubo (15 June 1991, VEI 6) injected around 20 megatonnes of SO₂ into the stratosphere, forming a sulphate aerosol veil.

Tambora (1815, VEI 7) caused the 'Year Without a Summer' in 1816 — crop failures across the Northern Hemisphere, snow in June in New England, the wet summer that kept Mary Shelley indoors at Lake Geneva writing 'Frankenstein'. Krakatoa (1883) produced red sunsets globally for years.

Toba (around 74,000 years ago, VEI 8) may have caused a population bottleneck in early humans, though this is debated.
items.why: Volcanic forcing is one of the strongest natural climate drivers on year-to-decade timescales. Climate models use these events as calibration points — the signal is large, well-dated and globally distributed.

items.title: An aftershock larger than the mainshock becomes the new mainshock
items.claim: What is the relationship between mainshocks and aftershocks?

options.text: Aftershocks are always at least one magnitude smaller

If a later quake in the sequence is larger, it is retrospectively called the mainshock and the earlier event becomes a foreshock — so by definition the named mainshock is the largest; aftershocks typically follow Båth's law (around 1.2 magnitudes smaller) and Omori's law (rate decays as 1/t)
Aftershocks are unrelated to the mainshock
All aftershocks occur within 24 hours

items.reveal:
Båth's law (1965) gives the largest aftershock as typically about 1.2 magnitudes smaller than the mainshock. Omori's law (1894) describes the rate decay: aftershocks fall off as 1/t after the main event.

The 2011 Christchurch earthquake (M6.3, 22 February 2011) was an aftershock of the September 2010 Darfield earthquake (M7.1). Because it was smaller, it kept the aftershock label — but it killed 185 people because it was shallower, closer to the city centre, and hit during business hours.

Aftershock sequences can continue for years after large events — the New Madrid 1811-12 sequence still produces detectable aftershocks two centuries later.
items.why: Statistical naming hides hazard. A 'smaller' aftershock can do more damage than its mainshock if its location and depth are worse — Christchurch is the canonical case.

items.title: Yellowstone caldera eruptions occurred at 2.1, 1.3 and 0.63 million years ago
items.claim: When have Yellowstone's largest eruptions occurred?

options.text: Every 10,000 years, with the last 100 years overdue

The three caldera-forming eruptions were Huckleberry Ridge (around 2.1 Ma), Mesa Falls (around 1.3 Ma) and Lava Creek (around 631 ka) — an average interval of around 725,000 years; the USGS sees no signs of imminent eruption
Last erupted in 1980 with Mount St Helens
Yellowstone is not a volcano

items.reveal:
USGS Yellowstone Volcano Observatory monitors ground deformation, seismicity and geyser activity continuously. The most recent lava flow at Yellowstone was around 70,000 years ago; the last major eruption (Lava Creek tuff) was 631,000 years ago.

Toba (Sumatra) erupted around 74,000 years ago, ejecting around 2,800 km³ of material — the largest known eruption in the last 25 million years. The Lava Creek eruption ejected around 1,000 km³.

A VEI 8 supereruption today would devastate North America with ash and disrupt global climate for years. The probability in any given year is very low — but not zero.
items.why: 'Overdue' supervolcano headlines misuse averages. Three datapoints do not define a periodic schedule; statistical interval is not a due date. The honest answer is 'we don't know when, but not soon based on monitoring'.

items.title: Around 80% of the Nile's flow comes from Ethiopian Highlands
items.claim: Where does most of the Nile's water originate?

options.text: Lake Victoria provides most of the flow

The Blue Nile (rising at Lake Tana in Ethiopia) and the Atbara, both fed by monsoonal rains in the Ethiopian Highlands, together contribute around 80-85% of annual discharge — concentrated in the July-October flood
Groundwater across Sudan
Rainfall directly over Egypt

items.reveal:
The White Nile drains Lake Victoria and the East African Plateau but loses much to evaporation in the Sudd swamps of South Sudan. Its contribution to the lower Nile is roughly 15-30% — and is more stable through the year.

The Blue Nile rises at Lake Tana (Ethiopia) and falls 1,300 m through steep gorges, fed by the Indian Ocean monsoon between June and September. The Atbara, dry through much of the year, contributes additional seasonal flow.

The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), filling since 2020, controls the dominant source — triggering serious dispute with Egypt and Sudan, whose 1929 and 1959 treaties allocated them most of the flow without Ethiopian involvement.
items.why: Water politics is geographically constrained. The Nile dispute makes no sense without knowing where the water comes from — and the 21st-century geopolitics of African dams cannot be understood without the underlying hydrology.

items.title: The 1931 China floods may be the deadliest natural disaster in recorded history
items.claim: What was the death toll of the 1931 China floods?

options.text: Around 100 — a localised flood

Estimates range from 422,000 to over 4 million dead — counting drowning, disease and famine after extreme monsoon rainfall on the Yangtze, Huai and Yellow river basins; likely the deadliest natural disaster of the 20th century
Around 10,000 dead
No reliable estimate exists

items.reveal:
The 1931 floods affected the Yangtze, Huai and Yellow river basins after exceptional monsoon rainfall. Chris Courtney's 'The Nature of Disaster in China' (2018) gives careful estimates: direct deaths from drowning around 150,000; deaths including subsequent disease and famine around 2 million.

Wuhan was submerged for weeks. The Republic of China government — distracted by the Japanese invasion of Manchuria the same September — was overwhelmed. Nanjing's Yangtze flood mark of 1931 is still visible.

The Three Gorges Dam (completed 2006) is partly justified as flood control; the 1931, 1954 and 1998 Yangtze floods all killed thousands.
items.why: River flooding remains the deadliest natural hazard category by long-term death toll. Vulnerability is not just hazard — it is state capacity, infrastructure and timing of other crises.

items.title: Meanders migrate downstream and laterally over time
items.claim: How do meanders change over time?

options.text: They are fixed channel features that do not change

Helical flow concentrates erosion on the outer bank (river cliff) and deposition on the inner bank (point bar); meanders migrate downstream and outward, eventually being cut off as oxbow lakes when meander necks are breached
Meanders migrate upstream against current
Meanders only form in glacial rivers

items.reveal:
The thalweg (line of fastest flow) traces an S-curve through meanders, swinging from outer bank to outer bank. Bank erosion rates can be 1-10 m/year in alluvial rivers — Mississippi meander cutoffs were mapped by Harold Fisk in 1944 for the US Army Corps of Engineers, showing channel migration across tens of km of floodplain over centuries.

The Corps now actively manages cutoffs to prevent further channel shortening. The Carter Lake oxbow (Iowa/Nebraska) is on the Iowa side of the modern Missouri River because of a single cutoff in 1877.

Floodplain land is dynamic. Property built on meander-prone rivers faces migration as well as flood risk.
items.why: Floodplains are not static. Long-term planning has to account for channel movement, not just discharge — a slower hazard but no less inevitable.

items.title: Bankfull discharge has a return period of around 1-2 years
items.claim: What is 'bankfull discharge'?

options.text: Annual mean flow

The discharge that fills the channel to the top of its banks — for most rivers, with a return period of around 1-2 years; this is the flow most responsible for channel shape (the 'dominant discharge')
A 1,000-year flood
The lowest flow on record

items.reveal:
Bankfull is the discharge at which water just begins to spill onto the floodplain. Wolman and Miller (1960) showed that this 'effective' discharge does most of the geomorphic work, because it combines moderate magnitude with sufficient frequency.

Flood frequency analysis fits a probability distribution (often Gumbel or GEV) to the annual maximum series. A 100-year flood has a 1% chance of occurring in any year — not a guaranteed schedule.

Flood Estimation Handbook methods (UK) and Bulletin 17C (US) standardise flood frequency analysis. Urbanisation 'flashifies' hydrographs — peak discharge rises and lag time falls.
items.why: Channels are shaped by frequent moderate floods, not rare catastrophes. Understanding bankfull discharge is essential for river management, restoration and floodplain mapping.

items.title: Global sea level is rising around 3.4 mm/year and accelerating
items.claim: How fast is global mean sea level rising?

options.text: Sea level has been stable for centuries
Satellite altimetry since 1993 shows an average of around 3.4 mm/year, accelerating since 2010; IPCC AR6 (2021) projects 0.28-1.01 m rise by 2100 depending on emissions scenario
Around 10 cm per year
Sea level is falling globally

items.reveal:
Thermal expansion of warming ocean water contributes about 40% of recent rise; melt from glaciers and ice sheets contributes the rest. Greenland's mass loss has risen from around 50 Gt/year in the 1990s to around 280 Gt/year in the 2010s (NASA GRACE).

Local sea-level rise can differ markedly from the global mean — isostatic rebound (Scotland rising), ocean dynamic processes (AMOC slowdown raising US East Coast levels), and subsidence (sinking deltas) all matter.

The IPCC AR6 SROCC (2019) and AR6 (2021) provide the standard reference. RCP8.5 scenarios with rapid Antarctic loss could exceed 2 m by 2100 — low probability, high impact.
items.why: Sea level rise is not uniform and not linear. Local coastal management must use regional projections, not a single global figure — and must include ice-sheet uncertainty as well as thermal expansion.

items.title: Sea walls cause 'coastal squeeze' that destroys intertidal habitat
items.claim: What is coastal squeeze?

options.text: Competition between coastal cities

When rising sea levels meet fixed hard defences, intertidal habitats (saltmarshes, mudflats) cannot migrate inland and are progressively drowned; managed realignment deliberately removes sea walls to let habitat re-form
Compression of coastal rocks by tides
Increased seasonal traffic at coastal resorts

items.reveal_title: Trapped between rising sea and hard wall
items.reveal:
Saltmarshes and mudflats provide flood protection (wave attenuation), biodiversity, carbon storage and fisheries nursery habitat. They normally accrete vertically and migrate inland as sea level rises — but only if there is space behind them.

Wallasea Island, Essex (2015) is the UK's largest managed realignment scheme, restoring 670 hectares of saltmarsh using soil from the Crossrail excavation. The Netherlands' 'Room for the River' programme (2007-2018) is the continental-scale equivalent.

Environment Agency Shoreline Management Plans now classify coast into 'no active intervention', 'managed realignment', 'hold the line' or 'advance the line' — a deliberately mixed strategy.
items.why: Hard engineering has ecological costs. 21st-century coastal management increasingly accepts deliberate retreat in some places to preserve habitat and reduce long-term defence costs.

items.title: Longshore drift can move entire beaches kilometres
items.claim: What does longshore drift do?

options.text: It moves sand directly out to deep water

Waves hit at an angle so swash carries sediment up the beach at that angle; backwash returns it straight down under gravity — net transport is along the coast, building spits and tombolos, stripping beaches downdrift of groynes
It only happens during storms
It transports sediment upstream in estuaries

items.reveal:
Spurn Head (East Yorkshire) is a 5 km spit built by longshore drift carrying sediment south from the eroding Holderness cliffs (retreating up to 2 m/year). The cliffs supply around 1 million m³ of sediment annually — much of it eventually ends up on Spurn or in the Humber estuary.

Groynes trap drift on their up-drift side. The downdrift side is starved of sediment, accelerating erosion. Coastal management at one beach can damage another — sediment budgets are zero-sum.

Dawlish Warren (Devon), Hurst Castle Spit (Hampshire), Slapton Sands (Devon) all illustrate dynamic spit-and-bar systems.
items.why: Coastal protection in one place can damage another. Understanding sediment budgets and littoral cells is essential to avoid simply moving the erosion problem along the coast.

items.title: Tides are driven by both the Moon and the Sun
items.claim: What causes spring and neap tides?

options.text: Only the Moon affects tides

The Moon provides about two-thirds of the tidal force, the Sun about one-third; when Sun, Earth and Moon align (new and full moon), tidal pulls combine for spring tides; at first/last quarter they oppose for neap tides — roughly fortnightly
Spring tides occur only in March-April
Tides are caused by Earth's rotation alone

items.reveal:
