The Moon's gravity raises a tidal bulge facing it (and another on the opposite side of the Earth). The Sun does the same but with one-third the force despite being much more massive — distance scales as the cube in tidal force.

At new and full moon (syzygy — alignment), the bulges add: spring tides, with the largest tidal range. At first and last quarter (90° angle), the Sun partly cancels the Moon: neap tides, smaller range.

The Bay of Fundy (Canada) has the world's largest tidal range, around 16 m. The Bristol Channel (Avonmouth) is second at around 15 m. 'Spring' here is from Old English 'springan' (to leap), not the season.
items.why: Etymological confusion can become factual confusion. Students often think spring tides only happen in spring; the actual mechanism is gravitational alignment, fortnightly, regardless of season.

items.title: The UK was under 1 km of ice at the Last Glacial Maximum
items.claim: How extensively was Britain glaciated around 20,000 years ago?

options.text: Only the Scottish Highlands had ice
The British-Irish Ice Sheet covered most of the country north of the Thames-Severn line, with ice up to 1 km thick over the Highlands; southern England was a permafrost tundra
All of Britain was permanently glaciated until 1500
Britain has never been glaciated

items.reveal:
The LGM (around 20,000 years ago) saw the British-Irish Ice Sheet extending to roughly the Thames-Severn line. Ice thickness over the Highlands exceeded 1 km. Glacial landforms record the maximum: corries (Snowdonia, Lake District), U-shaped valleys (Glencoe), drumlins (Eden Valley, Ribblesdale), erratics (the Norber erratics, Yorkshire).

The Younger Dryas (around 12,900-11,700 BP) was a final cold snap — the Loch Lomond Stadial — producing small Highland glaciers and ice caps. Britain was largely ice-free by around 10,000 years ago.

Britain rejoined Europe by land until the Storegga submarine landslide tsunami around 8,200 years ago finally severed Doggerland.
items.why: Most British landforms are products of the Quaternary Ice Ages, not earlier processes. The country's shape and soils are recent, contingent and shaped by ice.

items.title: Scotland is still rising — southern England is sinking
items.claim: What is glacial isostatic adjustment in the British Isles?

options.text: Britain has fully recovered from the Ice Age

Scotland and northern England rise by 1-2 mm/year as crust rebounds from glacial loading; southern and eastern England subside by around 1 mm/year as the forebulge collapses — both measured directly by GPS
All of Britain sinks equally
The motion is too slow to measure

items.reveal:
When the British-Irish Ice Sheet melted (around 10,000 years ago), the depressed crust began to rebound. Because the mantle behaves viscously over thousand-year timescales, the response is still ongoing.

The British Isles GNSS Facility (BIGF) measures vertical motion directly. Net result for relative sea level: southern England experiences faster sea-level rise than would be expected from climate alone, while northern Scotland experiences slower (or in some places falling) relative sea level.

Fenno-Scandinavia is rebounding even faster — up to 10 mm/year in parts of the Gulf of Bothnia. The Baltic Sea is gradually shrinking on the Scandinavian side.
items.why: Sea-level projections combine global climate signal with local geophysics. The Thames Barrier defends a coast that is itself sinking — accelerating the apparent rise.

items.title: Glaciers can move metres per day during surges
items.claim: How fast do glaciers move?

options.text: Glaciers are static features

Typically tens to hundreds of metres per year for valley glaciers; outlet glaciers like Jakobshavn (Greenland) reached around 17 km/year (around 46 m/day) in 2012; surge-type glaciers (around 1% of all glaciers) can move metres per day for months
Always 1 mm per year, too slow to detect
All glaciers move at the same uniform rate

items.reveal:
Glacier flow combines internal deformation (creep — ice flowing under its own weight, around 10-100 m/year for valley glaciers) and basal sliding (much faster when meltwater lubricates the bed).

Jakobshavn Isbrae drains around 7% of the Greenland Ice Sheet; its mass loss has been measured by satellite altimetry and GRACE. Variegated Glacier (Alaska) surged at around 65 m/day in 1982-83.

Climate warming has accelerated many outlet glaciers in Greenland and Antarctica — ice shelves at the front buttress the ice behind; when shelves break up, the ice behind speeds up. Pine Island and Thwaites (Antarctica) are the major current concerns.
items.why: Glacier dynamics control sea-level contribution. Flow speeds and acceleration mechanisms are central uncertainties in projecting 21st-century sea-level rise.

items.title: Each 1 mm of global sea level rise needs around 360 Gt of ice melt
items.claim: How does ice sheet mass loss translate into sea level rise?

options.text: Any amount of ice melt produces metres of rise

1 mm of global sea level rise requires around 360 Gt of ice; Greenland (around 280 Gt/year) plus Antarctica (around 150 Gt/year) currently contribute around 1.2 mm/year — about a third of total sea-level rise
Ice melt does not affect sea level
Only floating ice contributes to rise

items.reveal:
The global ocean surface area is around 360 million km². Spreading 360 Gt (360 × 10⁹ tonnes ≈ 360 km³) over that area gives roughly 1 mm rise.

NASA's GRACE (2002-2017) and GRACE-FO (since 2018) satellites measure ice mass directly via gravity changes. IPCC AR6 (2021) and IMBIE (2018, 2020) reconcile multiple methods.

Thwaites Glacier (the 'Doomsday Glacier') alone could raise global sea level by around 65 cm if it collapsed entirely. The West Antarctic Ice Sheet (WAIS) holds around 5 m of sea-level equivalent; Greenland holds around 7 m; East Antarctica around 53 m.
items.why: Sea-level rise has identifiable contributors. The arithmetic — area, volume, density — is straightforward; the unknown is how fast ice will leave the ice sheets, not what would happen if it did.

items.title: The Gulf Stream warms western Europe by an estimated 5 °C
items.claim: How much does ocean circulation warm western Europe?

options.text: Not at all — climate is determined by latitude alone

Comparison with similar-latitude locations (Calgary, Labrador) and modelling studies suggest the wider North Atlantic circulation system contributes around 5-10 °C of additional warmth to western Europe
By 30 °C — without it Europe would be like Antarctica
Less than 0.1 °C

items.reveal:
The Gulf Stream is the western boundary current of the North Atlantic gyre; it broadens north of Cape Hatteras into the North Atlantic Current. Prevailing westerlies carry the heat onshore.

Richard Seager and colleagues (2002) argued that atmospheric heat transport and the southwesterly stationary wave (set up by the Rocky Mountains) are at least as important as ocean heat in distinguishing western from eastern continental winters. The single-cause 'Gulf Stream warms Britain' story is too simple.

The AMOC (Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation) has weakened by an estimated 15% since the mid-20th century (Caesar et al., 2018, 2021). A collapse would cool Europe and warm the tropics.
items.why: Climate is the product of multiple systems acting together. The Gulf Stream story is partly true and partly simplified; a teaching answer needs both the ocean and the atmosphere.

items.title: The jet stream sits around 10 km up at the tropopause
items.claim: What is the jet stream?

options.text: A wind near the equator
A narrow band of fast westerly winds (typically 100-300 km/h) at around 9-12 km altitude, near the tropopause, driven by temperature contrasts between polar and tropical air masses
An ocean current in the Pacific
A jet of supersonic air over deserts

items.reveal:
The polar jet (which shapes UK weather) and the subtropical jet are the major Northern Hemisphere features. They meander in Rossby waves; the shape of those waves controls where storm tracks lie.

Jet streams were discovered by Japanese balloon-bombing campaigns of WWII and by US B-29 crews over the Pacific (1944) — flying west into apparently impossible headwinds. Carl-Gustaf Rossby's work in the 1930s-40s framed them theoretically.

Arctic amplification reduces the temperature contrast that drives the polar jet, possibly causing it to meander more — linked to more persistent weather extremes (heat domes, stuck storm tracks).
items.why: Surface weather has upper-atmosphere causes. Understanding why summer 2022 had heat domes or why winter 2013-14 had stuck Atlantic storm tracks requires looking at jet stream geometry.

items.title: The Arctic warms roughly 4 times faster than the global average
items.claim: What is Arctic amplification?

options.text: The Arctic warms at the same rate as the tropics
The Arctic has warmed roughly 4 times the global mean since 1979 (Rantanen et al., 2022), driven by ice-albedo feedback, water-vapour feedback and changes in heat transport
The Arctic is cooling overall
It happens only in winter

items.reveal:
Mika Rantanen and colleagues (Communications Earth & Environment, 2022) revised the long-cited 2× figure to nearly 4× for the Arctic Circle since 1979.

Ice-albedo feedback: snow and ice reflect around 80% of incoming solar radiation; open ocean absorbs around 90%. As sea ice retreats, more energy is absorbed and warming accelerates.

Arctic sea ice extent in September has fallen from around 7 million km² (1979 average) to under 4 million km² (recent minima). Downstream effects include changes to jet stream behaviour, ocean stratification and methane release from thawing permafrost.
items.why: Average warming hides extreme regional warming. The Arctic case shows how feedbacks multiply local signals — and why polar regions are decisive for global climate trajectory.

items.title: El Niño returns roughly every 2-7 years
items.claim: What is the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO)?

options.text: A single tropical storm in the Pacific
A coupled ocean-atmosphere oscillation in the tropical Pacific recurring every 2-7 years; El Niño (warm central/eastern Pacific) and La Niña (cool) reshape global rainfall, drought and storm patterns
An Atlantic Ocean current only
An annual cycle in the Arctic

items.reveal:
El Niño: weakened or reversed trade winds, warming of central and eastern equatorial Pacific, shifted convection. Typical effects: drought in Australia, Indonesia, parts of southern Africa; floods in coastal Peru and Ecuador; weaker Atlantic hurricane season; warmer global average.

La Niña: the opposite. The 1997-98 El Niño was among the strongest; 2015-16 contributed to record warm years and Great Barrier Reef bleaching.

Gilbert Walker first identified the Southern Oscillation atmospheric pattern in 1924 working with Indian Meteorological Department records. Jacob Bjerknes (1969) linked the atmospheric and oceanic components.
items.why: Global weather has oscillatory components. Forecasts months ahead are skilful when the ENSO state is known — and crops, water supplies and disaster planning across multiple continents depend on the call.

items.title: The Indian monsoon is driven by land-sea temperature contrast
items.claim: What causes the South Asian summer monsoon?

options.text: Earth's tilt alone
Differential heating: in summer the Asian continent (especially Tibetan Plateau) heats faster than the Indian Ocean, creating low pressure that draws in moist oceanic air; reversed in winter
Tropical cyclones combining each year
The Moon's gravitational pull

items.reveal:
From June to September, the Tibetan Plateau (the world's largest elevated land mass) heats intensely; low-level winds reverse and blow from the southwest, drawing moisture from the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal.

The Himalayas force orographic lifting, producing the wettest places on Earth: Mawsynram and Cherrapunji (Meghalaya) regularly receive over 11,000 mm/year. The Western Ghats provide a similar barrier for the south.

Around 1.5 billion people depend on the monsoon. The Indian Meteorological Department's onset dates have varied by weeks recently. Climate change is shifting onset and intensity in ways that are not yet well predicted.
items.why: Monsoon variability is one of the highest-stakes climate signals on Earth. A failed monsoon means famine; a strong one means floods. The driver (differential heating) is testable physics but the year-to-year variability is poorly forecast.

items.title: The Amazon generates much of its own rainfall
items.claim: How much of South American rainfall depends on Amazon transpiration?

options.text: None — rainfall comes entirely from the Atlantic

Amazon trees transpire huge volumes of water vapour, recycling moisture 5-6 times across the basin and generating 'flying rivers' that supply rainfall to southeast South America — including Brazil's agricultural heartland
Rainfall comes from Andean snowmelt
The Amazon receives no rainfall

items.reveal:
A mature Amazon tree can transpire 200-1,000 litres per day. The 'flying river' concept, popularised through INPE (Brazilian space agency) research and Antonio Nobre's work, describes the moisture flux from the basin southward — equivalent to or exceeding the Amazon River's surface discharge.

Deforestation reduces transpiration. Gatti et al. (Nature 2021) showed that the southern and eastern Amazon are already becoming net carbon sources. A tipping point at around 20-25% deforestation could shift large parts of the forest to savannah — with major consequences for Brazilian rainfall and agriculture.

Current deforestation is around 17-20% of the original Amazon area.
items.why: Forests are climate machines. Amazon loss would change rainfall patterns far beyond the basin — and threaten the agricultural economy that has driven much of the deforestation in the first place.

items.title: Most rainforest soils are highly weathered and nutrient-poor
items.claim: What surprises about tropical rainforest soil?

options.text: They are deep and extremely fertile

Heavy rainfall leaches soluble nutrients, leaving iron- and aluminium-rich oxisols (latosols); fertility is held in the biomass and recycled rapidly through litter — slash-and-burn agriculture works for only 2-3 years before fertility crashes
They are pure sand with no organic matter
All tropical soils are volcanic

items.reveal_title: Fertility in the trees, not the ground
items.reveal:
High rainfall and temperatures leach soluble nutrients (calcium, potassium, phosphorus) out of the upper soil, leaving heavily weathered, iron-rich red soils. Decomposition is rapid; mycorrhizal networks and shallow root mats intercept nutrients immediately.

Amazonian 'terra preta' (black earth) soils are a notable exception — anthropogenic soils created by pre-Columbian populations using charcoal, bone and food waste, retaining fertility for centuries. They are now studied as a biochar model.

When forest is cleared, the burn temporarily releases biomass nutrients; crops grow for 2-3 years before yields collapse.
items.why: Lush vegetation does not imply fertile soil. The 'rainforest = rich land' assumption has driven destructive agricultural expansion for centuries — and explains why cleared land degrades quickly.

items.title: Coral reefs fix nitrogen and support a quarter of marine species
items.claim: What is the ecological importance of coral reefs?

options.text: They are aesthetic features with little ecological role

Reefs cover under 0.1% of the ocean floor but host around 25% of marine species; symbiotic cyanobacteria fix atmospheric nitrogen, fertilising nutrient-poor tropical waters; reefs also protect coasts from wave energy
Reefs are made entirely of dead material
Reefs occur only in polar oceans

items.reveal:
Reefs occupy around 284,000 km² globally — under 0.1% of the ocean — and yet host an estimated 4,000 fish species, 800 reef-building coral species, and uncounted invertebrates.

Cyanobacteria in coral tissues and on reef surfaces fix atmospheric nitrogen, providing essential nutrients in otherwise oligotrophic (nutrient-poor) tropical waters. The reefs function as 'oases' of productivity.

Mass bleaching events (1998, 2010, 2014-17, 2024) have hit major systems. The Great Barrier Reef has bleached in 2016, 2017, 2020, 2022 and 2024. Estimated coastal protection value is tens of billions of dollars annually.
items.why: Concentrated biodiversity means concentrated risk. Losing reefs means losing entire ecosystems — not just iconic species — and removing coastal protection from hundreds of millions of people.

items.title: The boreal forest is the world's largest terrestrial biome
items.claim: Which is the world's largest forest biome?

options.text: Amazon tropical rainforest

The boreal forest (taiga) — a circumpolar belt across Russia, Canada, Alaska and Scandinavia totalling around 1.5 billion hectares; larger than all tropical rainforests combined and storing more carbon
Indonesian rainforest
European temperate woodland

items.reveal:
Boreal forest covers around 30% of all forest area and stores an estimated 30-40% of terrestrial carbon — much of it in deep peat and permafrost soils. Russia's taiga alone is around 12 million km².

Dominant species: spruce, fir, pine, larch, birch. Wildlife: brown bear, lynx, wolverine, capercaillie, moose. Productivity per hectare is lower than the Amazon, but the area is far larger.

Climate change is intensifying boreal wildfires — Siberia 2019-21, Canada 2023 — releasing carbon and potentially turning some boreal regions into net carbon sources. Permafrost thaw could release vast methane and CO₂.
items.why: The Amazon dominates public attention as 'the lungs of the planet'. The boreal forest is larger, stores more carbon, and is increasingly fire-prone — but receives a fraction of the press coverage.

items.title: Tokyo is the world's largest urban area at around 37 million
items.claim: How many megacities exist and which is largest?

options.text: Around 5 megacities, all in HICs
Around 33 megacities (cities over 10 million inhabitants) as of 2022; Tokyo is largest at around 37 million, followed by Delhi (32 m), Shanghai (28 m), Dhaka (23 m), São Paulo (22 m)
Around 100 cities, evenly distributed
Only Tokyo qualifies

items.reveal:
UN World Urbanization Prospects (2018, updated 2022) lists 33 megacities. Largest by metropolitan area: Tokyo (37 m), Delhi (32 m), Shanghai (28 m), Dhaka (23 m), São Paulo (22 m), Cairo (22 m), Mexico City (22 m), Beijing (21 m), Mumbai (21 m), Osaka (19 m).

Lagos (Nigeria, around 15 m) is the fastest growing — UN projections suggest it could exceed 30 m by 2050. By 2050, around 50 megacities are projected, most in Africa and South Asia.

Definitions matter: 'city proper' versus 'urban agglomeration' versus 'metropolitan area' produce different rankings.
items.why: The geography of global population has shifted. 19th-century urban hierarchies (London, Paris, New York) no longer describe reality. The major cities of the 21st century are largely in countries that were poor a generation ago.

items.title: Gentrification displaces existing residents through rising rents
items.claim: What is the mechanism of gentrification?

options.text: A purely positive process with no losers

Wealthier newcomers move into a previously disinvested neighbourhood; property prices and rents rise; existing lower-income residents (often disproportionately ethnic minority) are displaced — Neil Smith's 'rent gap' theory (1979) explains the economic mechanism
State demolition of all old housing
Spontaneous improvement without displacement

items.reveal:
Ruth Glass coined 'gentrification' in 1964 in 'London: Aspects of Change', describing the takeover of Islington working-class housing by middle-class incomers. Neil Smith's 'rent gap' theory (1979) explained the economic incentive: the gap between actual rent under disinvestment and potential rent after re-investment attracts capital.

London examples: Notting Hill (1960s onwards), Brixton (2000s), Hackney (2000s-2010s). Berlin: Prenzlauer Berg, Kreuzberg. New York: SoHo, Williamsburg.

Mitigation policies — affordable housing quotas, right-to-return clauses on estate redevelopment, rent control — have variable effectiveness. Sharon Zukin and others have argued the cultural displacement (loss of community) is as significant as the housing displacement.
items.why: Urban regeneration produces winners and losers. 'Rejuvenation' narratives obscure who is being displaced and who the city is being improved for — central to contemporary urban geography.

items.title: Around 90% of LIC employment is informal
items.claim: What share of work is informal in low-income countries?

options.text: Under 10%
Around 90% of employment in LICs and around 60% globally is informal (ILO 2018) — work without legal recognition, social protection or tax registration, totalling around 2 billion workers worldwide
Around 25% in all countries
Informal work is now extinct

items.reveal:
The International Labour Organization defines informal employment as work without legal recognition or social protection. Concentrations are high in sub-Saharan Africa (around 89% of non-agricultural employment) and South Asia (around 86%).

Main activities: street vending, waste-picking, small-scale agriculture, domestic work, informal manufacturing. Many informal workers are women; many have no fixed workplace.

Keith Hart's 1971 Accra fieldwork coined the modern use of 'informal sector'. ILO Recommendation 204 (2015) framed transition strategies to formal employment.
items.why: Models built on Global North wage labour misrepresent developing economies. The informal sector is not marginal — it is the modal experience of work for two billion people.

items.title: HDI combines health, education and income
items.claim: Why does the UN use HDI as well as GDP?

options.text: GDP is sufficient for all purposes

The Human Development Index (1990, devised by Mahbub ul Haq and Amartya Sen) combines life expectancy, education (mean and expected years of schooling) and GNI per capita — capturing health and education outcomes that GDP misses
HDI measures only government spending
HDI replaces all economic statistics

items.reveal:
The HDI uses three components — life expectancy, education, GNI per capita (PPP) — each normalised between 0 and 1, combined as a geometric mean (since 2010).

Top HDI rankings (2022): Switzerland, Norway, Iceland. UK 15th, US 21st. Bottom: Niger, South Sudan, Somalia. The Inequality-adjusted HDI (IHDI) drops the US further than the UK because of US within-country inequality.

The UN now also tracks the Gender Inequality Index (GII), the Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) and the SDG indicators. Critics: the HDI averages three different things and can obscure trade-offs.
items.why: What gets measured shapes priorities. A country that has converted wealth into health and education is a meaningfully different policy success than one with high GDP and poor outcomes.

items.title: The Brandt Line is now badly outdated
items.claim: Why is the Brandt Line increasingly criticised?

options.text: It is an active political boundary
Drawn for the 1980 Brandt Commission report, it placed South Korea, Singapore, Taiwan, UAE and Saudi Arabia in the 'poor South' — categories that 40 years of development have rendered misleading
A natural climatic boundary
An EU border

items.reveal:
The Brandt Commission's 'North-South: A Programme for Survival' (1980), led by former West German Chancellor Willy Brandt, drew a line dipping south to include Australia and New Zealand in the 'rich North'.

Since 1980: South Korea's GDP per capita has risen from around $1,700 to over $34,000; China's from $300 to $12,500; the Gulf states have grown dramatically. Meanwhile parts of southern and eastern Europe have stagnated.

Alternatives: World Bank country income classifications (low/lower-middle/upper-middle/high), the UN's Least Developed Country (LDC) list, the BRICS+ grouping, and the political-solidarity concept of the 'Global South' (distinct from the geographical Brandt Line).
items.why: Categories age. Using a 1980 division to describe the 2020s misses four decades of differential development. Geography teachers using Brandt without context perpetuate outdated assumptions.

items.title: Choropleth maps show areal data; isoline maps show continuous data
items.claim: What is the difference between choropleth and isoline maps?

options.text: There is no difference — alternative names for the same thing
Choropleth: defined areas (countries, counties) shaded by category. Isoline: lines connecting points of equal value (contours, isobars, isotherms, isohyets)
Choropleth shows only relief
Isoline maps cannot show climate data

items.reveal:
Choropleth maps assume uniform values within each area; they are vulnerable to the Modifiable Areal Unit Problem (MAUP) — different boundary choices produce different patterns.

Isoline maps (also called isarithmic) treat the variable as a continuous surface. Examples: contour lines (relief), isobars (atmospheric pressure), isotherms (temperature), isohyets (rainfall).

Other techniques: dot maps (each dot represents a count), proportional symbols (size scaled to value), flow lines (volume of movement), cartograms (areas distorted by value).
items.why: Map technique matters. The same data, mapped differently, tells different stories — and the right technique depends on whether the underlying variable is areal or continuous.

items.title: Stratified sampling deliberately includes defined subgroups
items.claim: Why use stratified sampling rather than random?

options.text: It is always quicker
Stratified sampling deliberately includes proportions from defined subgroups (e.g. age categories in a questionnaire, river sections by gradient), reducing the risk of missing minority categories
It produces fewer data points
It cannot be statistically analysed

items.reveal:
Sampling types: random (every member equally likely), systematic (every nth member — e.g. every 10 m along a river transect), stratified (proportional samples from defined groups), opportunistic (whoever is available — least rigorous).

GCSE and A-level NEA fieldwork requires explicit justification of sampling strategy. Small samples (n<30) limit statistical analysis; subgroup analysis needs larger samples in each stratum.

Fieldwork ethics — informed consent for questionnaires, minimising impact on study sites — has become more prominent in awarding-body specifications.
items.why: Bad sampling produces bad results regardless of subsequent analysis. Sampling design is upstream of every statistical inference — and is the most common point of failure in student fieldwork.

items.title: Standard deviation measures spread around the mean
items.claim: What does standard deviation tell you?

options.text: The highest value in the data
The typical (root mean square) deviation from the mean — about 68% of normally distributed data lies within one SD of the mean, 95% within two SD, 99.7% within three SD
The mean itself
Always equal to the range

items.reveal:
Standard deviation σ is calculated as the square root of the average squared deviation from the mean. For a normal distribution, the 68-95-99.7 rule applies — though many geographical datasets are not normal (skewed by extremes).

In fieldwork: comparing pebble sizes on two beaches, two questionnaire response distributions, or rainfall variability at two stations. A small SD means data cluster near the mean; a large SD means high variability.

Coefficient of variation (CV = SD/mean) allows comparison between datasets with different means — useful when comparing variability across scales.
items.why: Statistical literacy underpins geographical analysis. Reporting only a mean hides whether the data are tightly clustered or wildly variable — and the difference often matters more than the mean itself.

items.title: Spearman's rank correlation goes from -1 to +1
items.claim: What does Spearman's rank correlation coefficient measure?

options.text: Whether one variable causes another
The strength and direction of monotonic association between ranked variables, between -1 (perfect negative) and +1 (perfect positive); 0 indicates no monotonic relationship
The mean of the two variables
Only linear relationships

items.reveal:
Spearman's ρ uses ranks rather than raw values, making it robust to outliers and non-linear monotonic relationships. Pearson's r requires a linear relationship and normally-distributed data.

Critical values must be checked against sample size: with n=10, ρ must exceed about 0.564 to be significant at p=0.05. With n=30, the threshold is about 0.306.

A strong correlation can be coincidental, confounded by a third variable, or reversed in direction (Simpson's paradox). 'Correlation does not imply causation' is a methodological starting point, not a slogan.
items.why: Statistical reasoning is part of geographical skills. Strong correlation is evidence, not proof — geographers must argue causation separately from association, ideally through mechanism.

items.title: 4-figure grid references give 1 km precision; 6-figure give 100 m
items.claim: What precision do OS grid references provide?

options.text: Both give exact point locations

4-figure references identify a 1 km × 1 km square; 6-figure references identify a 100 m × 100 m square; 8-figure references give 10 m precision — read 'eastings before northings', 'along the corridor, up the stairs'
4-figure is more precise than 6-figure
References are accurate to 1 metre regardless

items.reveal:
OS uses a National Grid: read eastings (horizontal) first, then northings (vertical). Grid letters (NY, SE, etc.) identify 100 km squares.

A full reference combines letters with numerical eastings/northings — e.g. SE 543 367 for 100 m precision. The National Grid covers Great Britain; Northern Ireland uses the Irish Grid; the Channel Islands use UTM.

GPS coordinates (latitude/longitude or UTM) are international alternatives. Reporting accident or weather locations with inconsistent precision causes real navigation failures, including in search-and-rescue.
items.why: Map references are not arbitrary precision. Search and rescue, weather reporting and fieldwork all depend on consistent referencing — and the difference between 4 and 6 figures is the difference between 'somewhere in this 1 km square' and 'within a tennis court'.

items.title: OS contour lines show points of equal elevation
items.claim: What do OS contour lines show?

options.text: Roads and paths

Lines connecting points of equal elevation above sea level — close contours indicate steep slopes; OS 1:50,000 Landranger maps typically use 10 m intervals; 1:25,000 Explorer maps use 5 or 10 m intervals depending on relief
Property boundaries
Only rivers

items.reveal:
Closed loop contours with highest values inside indicate a hill summit. V-shaped contours pointing uphill indicate river valleys (water flows perpendicular to contours, downhill). Cliffs are shown by hachures or special vertical symbols.

Index contours (heavier lines) are labelled — typically every 50 m on 1:50,000 maps. Spot heights and trig points (triangulation pillars) give precise local elevations.

OS symbol conventions: black for human features, blue for water, brown for relief, green for vegetation, purple for tourist information. Knowing the key is half the skill.
items.why: Map literacy is portable across navigation, fieldwork and planning. Visual grammar (contour interval, symbol conventions) underpins all higher-level interpretation.

items.title: Cities are typically 2-5 °C warmer than surrounding countryside
items.claim: What is the urban heat island effect?

options.text: A myth — cities are no warmer than rural areas

Cities are typically 2-5 °C warmer than surrounding rural areas (up to 10 °C at night in extremes) due to dark surfaces (low albedo), reduced evapotranspiration, anthropogenic heat and reduced sky view
Cities are colder than countryside due to shade
Only New York shows the effect

items.reveal:
Causes: low-albedo asphalt and concrete absorb solar radiation; reduced vegetation cuts evaporative cooling; tall buildings trap re-emitted infrared (sky-view factor); waste heat from vehicles, buildings and air conditioning; thermal mass releases heat at night.

London during the August 2003 heatwave was around 4-9 °C warmer than surrounding countryside at night; UHI contributed to the death toll (around 2,000 excess deaths in the UK). Paris 2003 saw around 15,000 excess deaths.

Mitigation: green roofs, urban trees (Singapore, Melbourne), light-coloured surfaces (Los Angeles cool roofs), water features, ventilation corridors in city planning.
items.why: Urban climate is human-made microclimate. Climate change interacts with UHI to make heatwaves more dangerous in cities — a fast-rising public health hazard.
